claims.text: Cr or Al are examples of refractory-element additions suitable for the proposed lightweight HEA modification.
Adding 1–3 wt% Cr or Al during processing promotes in-situ formation of nanoscale oxide precipitates.
The resulting nanoscale oxide precipitates form preferentially at grain boundaries.
The nanoscale grain-boundary oxide precipitates are stable under the proposed testing or service conditions.
The oxide precipitates pin grain boundaries.
The oxide precipitates hinder dislocation motion.
Hindering dislocation motion increases the alloy's mechanical strength.
The grain-boundary oxide precipitates impede diffusion of oxygen into the alloy.
The grain-boundary oxide precipitates impede ingress or diffusion of corrosive species into the alloy.
Impeded oxygen diffusion improves high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Impeded transport of corrosive species improves corrosion resistance.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the refractory-modified alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the refractory-modified alloy will have a lower salt-spray corrosion rate.
Relative to the unmodified baseline, the refractory-modified alloy will exhibit lower weight gain during oxidation at 700–900°C.
The baseline alloy without deliberate refractory additions will lack the beneficial nanoscale oxide precipitates.
An excessively high refractory addition can produce coarse precipitates or phase separation.
Coarse precipitates or phase separation will cause the proposed strengthening and protective mechanism to cease to hold.
Temperatures or oxidation conditions beyond the stability limit of the nanoscale precipitates will cause the proposed mechanism to cease to hold.
